h1: Brewing a jamun fruit beer at home in the monsoon
title: Brewing a Jamun Fruit Beer at Home | Craft Beer School
desc: How to brew a jamun fruit beer in the monsoon: choosing and preparing the fruit, how much to add and how to avoid mould and wild yeast.
teaser: Jamun turns beer a deep purple and adds a tart, slightly astringent edge. The monsoon gives you the fruit and a mould problem at once.
standfirst: Jamun (Indian blackberry) arrives with the monsoon and gives beer a striking colour and a tart, dry finish. The humid season that brings the fruit also brings mould and wild yeast. Handling decides whether you get a fruit beer or an infection.
sections: Jamun is tart, astringent and very purple

Jamun, the fruit of Syzygium cumini, ripens in most of India from June to July. It is sweet and sour with a mouth-drying astringency from its tannins. It stains everything a deep purple.

In beer that profile works well in a light, low bitterness base. The tannin adds grip, the acid adds freshness and the colour does the marketing. The challenge is keeping the fruit flavour while controlling the astringency.
Pick a base beer that gets out of the way

A pale wheat beer or a simple blonde ale works best. For 20 litres at about 1.044:

  • 2.0 kg pilsner malt (50%)
  • 2.0 kg wheat malt (50%)
  • Mash at 65 °C for 60 minutes
  • Bitter to about 10 IBU, roughly 20 g of a 4% alpha hop at 60 minutes

Use a clean, neutral ale yeast. Avoid German wheat yeast, whose banana and clove notes compete with the fruit. Our wheat beer guide covers the base brew day.
Preparing the fruit in a humid season

Monsoon humidity means fruit can carry mould, wild yeast and bacteria. A clean process matters more than usual.

  1. Buy firm, fully ripe fruit with no split skins. Discard any soft or mouldy fruit.
  2. Wash in cold water and drain.
  3. Remove the large seeds. They add bitterness and extra tannin.
  4. Freeze the pulp and skins in sealed bags for at least 48 hours.

Freezing ruptures the cell walls so the fruit gives up flavour and colour faster. It also reduces, though does not eliminate, the wild microbes on the skin. Some brewers pasteurise the thawed pulp at about 70 °C for 10 to 15 minutes. That reduces microbes further but cooks off some fresh aroma.

A practical range is 100 to 200 g of prepared fruit per litre, so 2 to 4 kg for 20 litres. At 100 g per litre the colour is clear but the flavour is subtle. At 200 g per litre it tastes clearly of jamun with noticeable astringency.

Add the fruit after primary fermentation, once gravity has dropped close to final. Adding fruit to the boil cooks off aroma. Adding it to active primary sends much of the aroma out with the CO2. Put the thawed fruit in a sanitised mesh bag in a clean fermenter and rack the beer onto it.

The fruit adds sugar, so fermentation will restart. Expect several days of activity and some temperature rise. Ambient temperature in the monsoon often sits around 26 to 30 °C, which is high for clean ale yeast. Hold the fermenter around 18 to 20 °C with a water bath or fridge. Our guide to temperature control at home covers the options.

Leave the beer on the fruit for 7 to 10 days, then rack off. Check that gravity holds steady for at least three days before packaging. Fruit beers bottled early are a common cause of over-carbonated or bursting bottles.

Jamun colour starts deep purple and fades toward brownish red with time and oxygen. Keep headspace small, package with minimal splashing and drink the beer within a few months. If the beer tastes too drying, blend it with some unfruited base beer. Astringency softens a little with time, but colour fades too.

This is also a good beer to judge in a flight. Comparing different fruit levels side by side teaches you more about balance than any recipe.

Jamun is often linked with health benefits in Indian traditional practice. Beer is beer, so keep those claims off your label and out of your description. Talk about colour, tartness and season instead.
Keeping the batch sound in the wet season

Monsoon is the hardest season for sanitation at home. Kitchens stay damp, fruit flies arrive with the fruit and towels never quite dry. A few habits help:

  • Prepare the fruit in a clean, dry area away from open dustbins and drains.
  • Sanitise the mesh bag, the fermenter and anything the thawed fruit touches with a no-rinse sanitiser.
  • Fit an airlock or blow-off tube and keep fruit flies away from it; they carry acetic acid bacteria.
  • Check the surface of the beer when you rack. A white, wrinkled film or fuzzy spots mean contamination.

If a batch smells like vinegar or nail varnish, it has picked up bacteria or wild yeast. Do not bottle it. Taste the next batch more often and look for the gap in your process.
A one litre trial sets the fruit rate

When jamun arrives in your local market, buy 500 g, deseed it and freeze it. Thaw it into one litre of a light commercial beer for a week in the fridge and taste. That small trial tells you whether to aim for 100 or 200 g per litre before you commit a batch.
faqs: When should I add jamun to beer?
After primary fermentation, once gravity is close to final. That keeps more aroma than adding fruit to the boil or to active fermentation.
How much jamun do I need for 20 litres?
About 2 to 4 kg of prepared fruit, which is 100 to 200 g per litre.
